An em dash is a punctuation mark that looks like this: —

It is a long horizontal line, longer than a regular hyphen (-) or an en dash (–). It is called an "em dash" because, in traditional printing, it was made to be exactly as wide as the capital letter M.

You will often see it written without any spaces on either side—like this—especially in American writing. Some British writers put a space on each side — like this — but the no-space style is more standard globally.

The em dash is a powerful, versatile punctuation mark that you use when you want to interrupt, emphasize, explain, or separate something in a sentence. Think of it as a stronger, more dramatic version of a comma, a colon, or a pair of parentheses.

It signals to the reader: "Pay attention — something important is coming, or something just changed."
All the ways it is used

1. To add extra information in the middle of a sentence

This is its most common use. You can use a pair of em dashes (one on each side) to drop extra information into a sentence, almost like a whisper or a side note — but louder than parentheses.

She finally admitted the truth — the whole, embarrassing truth — after years of silence.

My dog — a scruffy little terrier — somehow unlocked the front door.

You could replace those em dashes with parentheses or commas, but the em dash feels more urgent and draws more attention.

2. To introduce an explanation or summary at the end of a sentence

Here, the em dash works like a colon, but it feels more casual and punchy. It says: "And here's the thing."

He wanted only one thing — revenge.

She packed everything she needed — sunscreen, a hat, water, and her camera.

The job was simple — too simple.

Compare this with a colon: "He wanted only one thing: revenge." Both are correct, but the em dash feels sharper and more conversational.

3. To show a sudden interruption or break in speech

In dialogue (when writing conversations), em dashes show that someone was cut off mid-sentence, either by another person or by a sudden action.

"I was just trying to explain—"
"I don't want to hear it," she snapped.

"If you would just listen for one—" The door slammed before he could finish.

Notice the em dash comes right after the last word, with no period. The sentence just stops — because that is exactly what happened.

4. To show a sudden change of thought

If a speaker or narrator suddenly shifts direction mid-thought, the em dash marks that pivot.

I was going to say yes — but then I remembered what happened last time.

Let me think — no, actually, I've already made up my mind.

5. To replace words like "that is," "namely," or "in other words"

She had one real weakness — chocolate.

There was one person who always believed in him — his mother.

This use creates a dramatic pause before the reveal.

6. To show missing or censored content

Occasionally, you will see em dashes used to replace a name, a word, or letters that are hidden on purpose.

He signed the letter "— — —" and never identified himself.

The suspect, Mr. —, was not available for comment.

This is a more old-fashioned or literary use, but you will still see it.
Em dash vs. hyphen vs. en dash

These three are often confused, so here is a simple breakdown:

  • Hyphen (-) — the shortest. Used to join words together: well-known, mother-in-law, self-aware. Also used to split a word at the end of a line.
  • En dash (–) — medium length. Used mainly for ranges and spans: pages 12–45, 2010–2020, Monday–Friday. Also used in compound adjectives where one part is two words: New York–based company.
  • Em dash (—) — the longest. Used for all the grammatical and stylistic purposes described in this article.

The key rule: if you are joining two words into one, use a hyphen. If you are showing a range, use an en dash. If you are interrupting, emphasizing, or adding a dramatic pause to a sentence, use an em dash.
How to type an em dash

• Mac: Press Option + Shift + - (the hyphen key)
  • Windows: Hold Alt and type 0151 on the numeric keypad (with Num Lock on), then release Alt
  • Microsoft Word / Google Docs: Type two hyphens (--) between two words without spaces, and the program will often auto-convert it to an em dash
  • Any device: You can copy-paste the symbol — from somewhere you have already seen it

The em dash is considered slightly informal or conversational compared to a colon. Because of this, it appears more in journalism, fiction, and casual writing than in formal academic papers, though it is not wrong in formal writing.

It also creates emphasis and rhythm. Read these two sentences aloud:

She had one dream (becoming an astronaut) since childhood.
She had one dream — becoming an astronaut — since childhood.

The second sentence has more punch. The em dashes slow the reader down and frame the information dramatically.
A word of caution: don't overuse it

Because the em dash is dramatic and attention-grabbing, using it too many times in one piece of writing weakens its effect. If every sentence has an em dash, none of them feel special anymore. Use it when you mean it — when you want that pause, that emphasis, that interruption to truly land.

The em dash (—) is a long punctuation mark used to:

  1. Insert a side note or extra detail mid-sentence (using a pair of em dashes)
  2. Introduce an explanation or climax at the end of a sentence
  3. Show that speech was cut off or interrupted
  4. Mark a sudden change of thought
  5. Replace words like "that is" or "namely" before a reveal
  6. Occasionally stand in for missing or hidden words

It is stronger than a comma, more casual than a colon, and more visible than parentheses. Its job is to create emphasis, drama, and a sense of interruption or urgency in writing.
